strengths: Novel and well-motivated integration of neuron attribution (importance) scores into model fusion. The paper demonstrates this helps not only its own methods but also improves baselines when retrofitted (e.g., Git Re-Basin jumps from 53.8 to 71.8 in Table 11), which is a convincing, transferable insight.

Principled formulation of fusion as representation matching with a clean decomposition into grouping and approximation error (Theorem 1), plus theoretical guarantees (optimality for Hungarian Fusion; a (9+epsilon) approximation for K-means Fusion via Kanungo et al.). The proofs in Appendix A appear correct.

Strong and consistent empirical results in the target regimes. In non-IID VGG11/CIFAR-10 (Table 1) the method reaches 84.6 vs. base models 81.5/75.1 and baselines OTFusion (43.4) and Git Re-Basin (71.8); in sharded ViT/CIFAR-100 (Table 2) it reaches 49.4 vs. base models 37.9/36.6. These are large, meaningful gains over prior fusion methods.

The framework generalizes to arbitrary architectures (VGG11 and ViT) and arbitrary (non-linear) layer types, with closed-form linear and SGD-based gradient variants, going beyond OTFusion's linear-layer restriction.

Reasonable reproducibility: open-source code, detailed appendices on data partitioning, training, fusion hyperparameters, and runtime, plus an honest limitations section and broader-impact discussion.
weaknesses: Reporting the 'best-performing importance score' per algorithm (Section 5.2) is a form of test-set selection that can inflate comparisons. The gap between uniform and best scores is large for HF Linear (72.3 vs. 84.6 in Table 11), so it is unclear whether the headline numbers reflect a fair, protocol-consistent comparison.

Presentation is sloppy in places: multiple reference errors (e.g., Bottou and Bengio cited as 1994 but listed 2018; Hinton et al. cited as 2015 but listed 2023; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber listed as 'Hochreiter and Hinton 2023'; Dhamdhere et al. cited as 2018 but listed 2020), and confusing/misaligned table rows (e.g., the 'Efficiency'/'Inference Cost' rows in Tables 3 and 10).

Computational cost is substantially higher than baselines (Table 6: KF Linear 78.3s vs. OTFusion 0.7s and Git Re-Basin 1.0s), and the gradient variant scales poorly with fusion data (Table 7: 38.1s at 400 samples vs. 632.5s at 6000 samples), limiting practicality.

Generality claims are only partially supported: in the full-dataset setup the fused model underperforms base models zero-shot (Table 3: -0.7 and -2.5), and after fine-tuning the gains are marginal (+0.6/+0.3). This undercuts the claim of broad applicability across regimes.

The term 'zero-shot' is used loosely: the gradient variant trains the fused model level-by-level, and even the linear variant requires fitting targets per level; this is not zero-shot in the usual sense and should be characterized more precisely.

Baseline coverage is limited to somewhat dated methods (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin) plus vanilla averaging and last-layer KD; relevant recent fusion/aggregation methods (e.g., FedMA and newer transformer-fusion work) are not empirically compared, and OTFusion-Transformer could not be run, leaving the strongest related comparison incomplete.

The gradient variant is acknowledged to be sensitive to hyperparameters, relying on two ad hoc 'settings' that were empirically found to generalize; the dependence of reported results on this selection is not fully disentangled.

strengths: Introduces a principled two-step decomposition of neuron-level model fusion into grouping and approximation errors, enabling the use of Hungarian matching, K-means clustering, and closed-form/SGD fitting. The formulation is intuitive and flexible across layer types.

Incorporates neuron attribution scores into both clustering and approximation, with empirical gains in non-IID settings (e.g., HF Linear improves from 72.3 to 84.6 on VGG non-IID 2-way when using conductance/DeepLIFT).

Provides theoretical analysis: Theorem 1 gives a clean decomposition; Theorem 2 offers optimality for Hungarian fusion and a (9+ε)-approximation for K-means fusion under affine levels and local-search clustering.

Experiments cover multiple regimes (non-IID, sharded, full-dataset) and architectures (VGG11, ViT), with comparisons to OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, vanilla averaging, last-layer KD, and ensembles. In non-IID VGG experiments, the proposed methods substantially outperform prior fusion baselines and approach ensemble performance.
The limitations section honestly discusses hyperparameter sensitivity, dependence on fusion data size, and runtime concerns.
weaknesses: Critical experimental flaw in the sharded setup: fusion data is described as 'sampled from the dataset seen by the first model' (Tables 2, 9, 13), but in sharded partitions each model sees only a disjoint subset of classes. It is unclear how the fused model can preserve knowledge of classes absent from the fusion data, yet reported accuracies are far above base models and near ensemble. This raises serious doubts about the validity of the sharded results; if the data actually covered all classes, the description is incorrect and must be fixed.

Missing key baselines: OTFusion and Git Re-Basin are not compared on ViT experiments (non-IID, sharded, full-dataset), despite being the main prior fusion methods. The claim of consistently outperforming previous fusion techniques is therefore not fully supported.

Theoretical guarantees are limited and mismatched with the algorithm: Theorem 2 only applies to affine levels, is per-layer, and assumes local-search K-means while the implementation uses Lloyd's algorithm. The proof for K-means relies on projecting base activations onto the column space of previous fused activations, but the theorem statement does not mention this projection. No global network-level guarantee or error-propagation analysis is provided.

Computational cost is high: runtime tables show KF Linear takes 78.3s vs OTFusion 0.7s and Git Re-Basin 1.0s for VGG; KF Gradient on ViT takes 632.5s for 6000 samples. This practical drawback is not adequately addressed.

Presentation issues and citation errors are pervasive: e.g., 'Bottou and Bengio [2018]' vs 1994, 'Hinton et al. [2023]' vs 2015, 'Hochreiter and Hinton [2023]' vs 1997, inconsistent table entries (Table 1 vs Table 11 for 8-way base models), missing code URL ('The code is available at:' blank). These hinder clarity and reproducibility.

The greedy, layer-wise optimization lacks theoretical justification for the full network: matching cluster centers level-by-level does not guarantee improved final outputs, and the paper does not analyze how approximation errors accumulate across levels.

The comparison to knowledge distillation may be unfair: full KD was restricted to the last layer due to overfitting, and KD is not a zero-shot fusion method, so zero-shot comparisons are not apples-to-apples.

The claim of being 'first to successfully incorporate neuron importance scores in model fusion' is questionable, as OTFusion already used neuron importance as a probability measure in its optimal transport formulation, as acknowledged in Appendix C.

Generality is not fully demonstrated: only VGG11 and ViT on CIFAR-10/100 are tested; no ResNets, other Transformer variants, or larger-scale datasets. The claim of supporting arbitrary layer types and architectures is thus only partially evidenced.

strengths: Introduces a principled neuron-centric model fusion framework that decomposes the representation matching objective into interpretable grouping and approximation errors, leading to a natural two-stage algorithm.

Successfully incorporates neuron attribution scores into the fusion process, demonstrating consistent empirical gains and showing that the idea can be retrofitted to existing methods such as Git Re-Basin.
Handles arbitrary differentiable architectures via a gradient-based variant, as demonstrated on ViTs, while also providing an efficient closed-form solution for affine levels.

Provides theoretical guarantees for the linear case: Hungarian Fusion is optimal for one-to-one equal-size matching, and K-means Fusion achieves a (9+epsilon)-approximation under local-search clustering.
Strong zero-shot results on non-IID and sharded setups, substantially outperforming OTFusion, Git Re-Basin, and last-layer KD, and approaching ensemble-level accuracy in several settings.
Good reproducibility practices: code is available, data partitioning, hyperparameters, and implementation details are documented, and limitations plus broader impact are discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the grouping/approximation decomposition is a standard algebraic identity, and importance-weighted neuron matching has precedent in OTFusion. The claim of being the first to incorporate neuron importance scores is overstated.

Evaluation may select the best importance score per algorithm based on test accuracy rather than a validation set, which undermines the zero-shot claim and can inflate comparisons, especially for Hungarian Fusion where uniform vs. conductance scores differ dramatically.

Missing comparisons to directly relevant baselines such as FedMA, Transformer OTFusion, and recent model-merging methods (e.g., TIES, DARE, RegMean) limit positioning and confidence in the claimed superiority.

The theoretical decomposition assumes a fixed assignment, but the algorithm clusters base activations without jointly optimizing the fused outputs; thus the approximation step may not preserve the minimum-distance assignment, and the guarantee is layer-wise and only for linear levels.
Full-dataset results are marginal: zero-shot fused models often fall slightly below base models, and fine-tuning only barely surpasses base models while remaining well below ensembles.
Evaluation is limited to VGG11/ViT on CIFAR-10/100; no larger-scale or diverse architecture/dataset validation is provided.
Runtime is substantially slower than OTFusion and Git Re-Basin (e.g., K-means Linear Fusion takes ~78s vs. ~0.7s for OTFusion on VGG), which may limit practical adoption.
Presentation has numerous typos, citation year errors (e.g., Hinton et al. 2023 for a 2015 paper), vague pseudocode details, and a proof typo in Appendix A, reducing clarity and polish.

strengths: Introduces a principled two-stage neuron-centric fusion framework that casts fusion as representation matching: cluster base-model neurons into targets and retrofit the fused model to match importance-weighted centroids. The method is flexible and applies to VGGs, ResNets, and ViTs, and supports more than two models, different widths, and different depths.

Incorporates neuron attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into the clustering/alignment step, with an empirical analysis of how non-uniform importance shifts cluster assignments. This is a useful direction for preserving salient features during fusion.

Provides a theoretical decomposition of the representation cost into grouping and approximation errors (Theorem 1) and offers guarantees for the Hungarian and K-means variants under linear/fixed-previous-level assumptions (Theorem 2).

Extensive empirical evaluation across sharded, non-IID, full-dataset, compression, and different-width settings. The strongest results are in zero-shot sharded/non-IID regimes, where the proposed methods substantially outperform OTFusion and often approach ensemble performance (e.g., BloodMNIST).

Includes an open-source reimplementation, detailed hyperparameters, and supplementary results, which supports reproducibility. The limitations section and impact statement are honest and discuss hyperparameter sensitivity, data efficiency, and runtime.
The method is architecturally modular and can be applied to any DAG-of-levels decomposition, making it more general than many prior pairwise or layer-specific fusion methods.
weaknesses: The novelty claim around neuron importance is overstated: OTFusion (Singh & Jaggi, 2020) already used neuron importance as a probability measure in optimal transport, as the authors themselves acknowledge in Appendix C. Claiming to be the first to incorporate neuron importance scores is inaccurate and should be softened to a claim about attribution-based scores in clustering/retrofitting.

The term 'zero-shot' is debatable for the gradient-based variants: they train the fused model on the fusion dataset during fusion, whereas OTFusion and Git Re-Basin use data only for alignment. This gives the method additional optimization capacity and may not be directly comparable. The paper should clearly distinguish alignment-only zero-shot fusion from fusion with gradient training.

The theoretical guarantees do not fully match the implementation. Theorem 2(b)'s (9+epsilon) bound assumes local-search K-means, but the experiments use Lloyd's algorithm. The gradient variants also use plain MSE rather than the importance-weighted MSE derived from the objective, so the algorithm does not exactly optimize the stated representation cost.

In the non-IID VGG/CIFAR-10 experiments (Appendix Table 13), Linear Probing (LP) outperforms the proposed full method for 4-way and 8-way splits (e.g., LP 81.4 vs KF-Linear 79.5 and KF-Gradient 77.8 for 4-way), which contradicts the claim of consistent improvements over baselines. This should be discussed explicitly in the main text rather than left to the appendix.

The empirical comparison omits several standard recent model-merging baselines (e.g., TIES, DARE, RegMean, Fisher merging, CART). While some are designed for fine-tuned models, including at least a subset would strengthen the evaluation and situate the contribution more clearly in the current literature.

Presentation has several issues: typos such as 'keep the weights of keep the weights', inconsistent notation (d^M vs d^F), reference year errors, and some main-text tables are incomplete or lack standard deviations. The level-partitioning choice is heuristic and not systematically studied.

Some hyperparameter details are not fully explained (e.g., 'Perturbation ε = 1.0' in Table 9), which may hinder exact reproduction. The fusion dataset in sharded/non-IID settings is drawn from one base model; while motivated by FL privacy, this choice may be overly optimistic and should be stress-tested with other public or out-of-distribution fusion data.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: model fusion under non-IID, sharded, and zero-shot settings, with relevance to federated learning and privacy-preserving model reuse.
Proposes a flexible neuron-centric fusion framework (HF/KF) that can be applied to VGGs, ResNets, and ViTs, supports more than two models, and handles different widths/depths via k-means clustering.
Incorporates neuron attribution scores (Conductance, DeepLIFT) into alignment/clustering, an interesting and underexplored direction in model fusion.
Provides a theoretical decomposition of the representation cost (Theorem 1) and an approximation bound for KF under linear levels (Theorem 2), though limited in scope.
Empirical results on VGG non-IID/sharded CIFAR-10 and BloodMNIST show large zero-shot gains over OTFusion and Git Re-Basin; KF-Linear reaches 91.0% on BloodMNIST versus 88.4% for the ensemble.
ResNet compression results are strong: KF-Gradient achieves 70.6% (ResNet-34 to ResNet-18) versus 45.9% for KD with only 5k samples.
The appendix is extensive, with hyperparameters, runtime analysis, and additional results; an open-source reimplementation is intended.
Includes a limitations section discussing hyperparameter sensitivity, data efficiency, and runtime overhead.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'consistent improvements over existing fusion methods' is contradicted by the paper's own results: in Table 2, KD outperforms KF-Gradient on 4-way (47.0 vs. 41.4) and 6-way (43.6 vs. 34.7) sharded ViT CIFAR-100. The text highlights OTFusion's collapse but does not acknowledge that a stronger baseline (KD) beats the proposed method in these settings, which is selective reporting.

The comparison to Transformer OTFusion is unfair in the ViT experiments: OTFusion uses only 200 fusion samples (due to OOM in the authors' implementation) while the proposed KF/HF methods use 5000 samples (Tables 2, 5, 6, 17–20). Since performance clearly scales with fusion dataset size (Tables 4 and 7), the claimed zero-shot gains are confounded by a large data advantage.

The term 'zero-shot' is misleading. The gradient variants train each level of the fused model for up to 100 epochs on the fusion dataset (Table 9), so they are trained fusion methods, not zero-shot methods. Comparing them to untrained OTFusion/Git Re-Basin is not apples-to-apples; the setting should be described as 'without post-fusion fine-tuning' and compared against equally trained baselines.

The ZipIt! comparison forces all layers, including classification heads, to be zipped, which is not ZipIt!'s intended use. The paper acknowledges degraded performance in this setting but still uses it as a main baseline, overstating the practical advantage.

Novelty is incremental: the method combines known ideas such as Hungarian/OT-based neuron matching, k-means clustering of activations, activation matching, and intermediate knowledge distillation/retrofitting. OTFusion already uses importance scores as probability measures in optimal transport, so the claim of being the first to successfully incorporate neuron importance scores is overstated.

Theoretical guarantees do not align with the actual algorithm: Theorem 2 relies on the Kanungo et al. local-search (9+ε) algorithm, but the practical KF implementation uses Lloyd's algorithm, so the approximation bound does not apply. Theorem 1 is essentially a standard bias-variance/k-means decomposition and is not a deep technical contribution.

The manuscript contains technical and presentational errors: Equation (3) sums over d^M instead of d^F; the proof has typos and inconsistent indices; reference years are wrong (e.g., Theus et al. 2026, Sundararajan et al. 2026); phrases like 'keep the weights of keep the weights' and garbled text appear; and the code URL is missing from the abstract and appendix.

Important controls and baselines are missing: full-dataset ViT experiments omit LP/KD, ImageNet ResNet experiments omit KD, and ViT sharded experiments do not run KF with 200 samples to match OTFusion's data budget. There is no analysis of why KD outperforms KF for >2 ViT clients, despite the paper claiming robustness as sharding increases.

Some key results are high variance or based on limited seeds (e.g., BloodMNIST KF-Linear 91.0 ± 2.7 versus ensemble 88.4 ± 3.0 is not statistically significant; 4-way ViT full-dataset results use a single seed). Strong claims such as surpassing ensemble performance are therefore not well supported.

Baseline tuning appears problematic: OTFusion with importance scores performs worse than OTFusion without them in Table 13 (49.6 to 40.6), suggesting implementation/tuning issues rather than a fundamental limitation. This weakens the claim that importance scores enhance existing methods.

The practical advantage is narrower than claimed: HF only handles pairwise equal-sized models, while KF handles general cases but underperforms KD for >2 ViT clients. The architecture flexibility claim is therefore not fully realized in the most challenging heterogeneous settings.

strengths: Introduces a principled neuron-centric fusion framework that casts fusion as representation matching with importance-weighted clustering and retrofitting, enabling fusion of architectures modularizable as DAGs (VGGs, ResNets, ViTs) and supporting more than two models, different widths, and compression.
Provides a useful theoretical decomposition (Theorem 1) and guarantees for HF and KF under affine assumptions, offering interpretable grouping/approximation errors.

Extensive empirical evaluation across full-dataset, non-IID, and sharded regimes, multiple architectures, importance scoring methods, and baselines; shows strong zero-shot gains in several settings and improved compression over KD.
Open-source code and detailed hyperparameters/implementation details support reproducibility; limitations are discussed honestly.
The method is flexible and the two-stage design is simple to implement and adapt.
weaknesses: Major experimental inconsistency: in sharded setups, fusion data is stated to come from one base model's disjoint classes, yet fused models achieve accuracy far above the theoretical maximum if the other classes are never seen (e.g., BloodMNIST 91.0% on all 8 classes using only 400 samples from 6 classes; VGG CIFAR-10 2-way 80.9% using only the first model's 5 classes; ViT CIFAR-100 54.4% when the first model sees only 50 classes). This suggests data leakage, mis-specified sharding, or an incorrect description of the fusion data. Without clarification, the central zero-shot sharded results are not credible.

The term 'zero-shot' is misleading: the gradient-based variants optimize the fused model's weights via SGD on a fusion dataset (Algorithm 1), so they are training/retrofitting procedures, not training-free fusion. Comparisons against training-free baselines (OTFusion, Git Re-Basin) in zero-shot tables conflate different levels of data use and training.

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 2(b)'s (9+epsilon) guarantee relies on the local-search algorithm of Kanungo et al. and weighted K-means, but the implementation uses Lloyd's algorithm and plain MSE in gradient variants; the closed-form solution in Appendix B.2 appears inconsistent with the derived weighted approximation error (S matrix usage), and the proof/equations contain typos (e.g., d^M vs d^F, extra s_j factor).
Missing critical implementation details for ViTs: how sequence/token dimensions are handled when treating embedding dimensions as neurons is not explained, hindering reproducibility.

Overclaims relative to evidence: Table 1 claims support for different depths but no fusion experiment with different depths is shown; 'first to successfully incorporate neuron importance scores' is overstated given OTFusion already uses importance in optimal transport; full-dataset fine-tuned results do not consistently outperform OTFusion/Git Re-Basin (e.g., Table 15 VGG CIFAR-10 OTF fine-tuned 93.2-93.5 vs KF-Gradient 93.0-93.2).
Scalability and efficiency concerns: runtime for KF-Linear is ~78s vs OTFusion ~0.7s for small VGGs; no LLM or large-scale evaluation; hyperparameter sensitivity of gradient variants remains.
Some baselines are missing or incomplete: REPAIR for Git Re-Basin and FedMA are not compared; Git Re-Basin fine-tuned results are omitted in full-dataset tables.
